result: The Multiethnic Cohort (MEC) was established in 1993-1996 and has followed over 215,000 residents of Hawaii and Los Angeles aged 45-75 at recruitment, including five main racial/ethnic groups (African American, Japanese American, Latino, Native Hawaiian, and White), with approximately 100,000 members (median age 82) still alive as of 2019.
evaluation: Claims C19-C22 provide consistent descriptive information about the MEC cohort establishment, size, composition, and survival that is directly stated in the manuscript and supported by appropriate citations (Kolonel et al., 2000). These foundational cohort characteristics are well-documented.

result: A total of 6,974 MEC members completed the baseline COVID-19 survey (6,068 online, 906 paper) between May-September 2020, with 43.5% men and 56.5% women. Response rates were low overall (7.2% men, 6.3% women), with White participants having the highest response rates (13.2% men, 12% women) followed by Japanese American, Native Hawaiian, Other, African American, and Latino groups.
evaluation: Claims C23-C29 present straightforward descriptive statistics about survey participation that are directly reported in the manuscript with clear numerical data. The response rates and demographic breakdown are explicitly stated and internally consistent.

result: The COVID-19 survey sample was not fully representative of the entire MEC cohort, with survey respondents being more educated, having larger representation of Whites and Japanese Americans, smaller representation of Latinos and African Americans, and very low representation of those in retirement/care homes (0.9% men, 1.7% women).
evaluation: Claims C98-C100 acknowledge important limitations in the representativeness of the survey sample, supported by comparison with the 2019 MEC survivor cohort (Supplementary file 1). These are appropriate self-critical assessments of selection bias that are well-documented in the manuscript.

result: During the COVID-19 pandemic, 78.8% of men and 84.4% of women reported making lifestyle changes. Small percentages reported changes in drinking behavior (4.2% men and 4.3% women drinking more; 6.3% men and 5.2% women drinking less), and only 3.7% of men and 2.6% of women were current smokers.
evaluation: Claims C30-C33 report descriptive survey results that are directly stated in the manuscript. The percentages are clearly presented and internally consistent, representing straightforward behavioral data from the survey responses.

result: During the COVID-19 pandemic, 54.2% of men and 61.2% of women postponed regular healthcare visits (most frequently primary care physician and dentist visits), while 5.7% of men and 11.0% of women postponed cancer screenings (most frequently mammography, skin examination, and colorectal screening). Among 917 participants diagnosed with cancer in the past 5 years, 238 were currently receiving treatment, with 11.5% of men and 6.9% of women canceling at least one treatment session.
evaluation: Claims C34-C40 present descriptive statistics about healthcare disruptions that are directly reported in the manuscript with references to Tables 2 and 3. The data are internally consistent and clearly documented, though the low overall screening postponement rates (5.7-11.0%) are noted by the authors as lower than expected.

result: Multivariable logistic regression analysis identified significant associations with making lifestyle changes during COVID-19: by race/ethnicity (Native Hawaiian and Other men/women less likely, African American men more likely vs. Whites), by age (2-3% less likely per year), by sex (women 62% more likely), by education (10-12% more likely per year), and by comorbidities (those with heart disease, hypertension, or lung disease more likely).
evaluation: Claims C41-C55 report results from multivariable logistic regression models (Table 4) with appropriate odds ratios, confidence intervals, and p-values. The statistical approach is appropriate for the cross-sectional survey design, though the models adjust for multiple variables simultaneously which is properly documented.

result: Multivariable logistic regression analysis identified significant associations with postponing regular healthcare visits: by race/ethnicity (Latino and Native Hawaiian men, Native Hawaiian women less likely vs. Whites), by age (women 2% less likely per year), by sex (women 43% more likely), by education (men 4% more likely per year), and by comorbidities (men with heart disease, women with hypertension/kidney disease/recent cancer diagnosis more likely).
evaluation: Claims C56-C65 report results from multivariable logistic regression models (Table 5) with appropriate statistical measures. The analysis is methodologically sound for identifying factors associated with postponing healthcare visits, with proper adjustment for confounders.

result: Multivariable logistic regression analysis identified significant associations with postponing cancer screening: by race/ethnicity (Japanese American men 72% less likely, Japanese American women 40% less likely vs. Whites), by age (women 4% less likely per year), by sex (women 137% more likely), by education (women 10% more likely per year), and by comorbidities (men and women with recent cancer diagnosis 254% and 222% more likely, respectively; women with lung disease 50% more likely).
evaluation: Claims C66-C73 report results from multivariable logistic regression models (Table 6) with appropriate statistical measures. The finding that those with recent cancer diagnoses were much more likely to postpone screening is notable and well-documented, though the authors acknowledge the low overall screening postponement rates limit interpretation.

result: Summary findings indicate that women with more education, women with lung disease/COPD/asthma, and individuals diagnosed with cancer in the past 5 years were more likely to postpone cancer screening, while older women and Japanese American men and women were less likely to postpone screening compared to their respective reference groups.
evaluation: Claims C89-C93 provide accurate summary statements of the main findings from the regression analyses (C66-C73, C68-C73). These summaries correctly synthesize the key results regarding factors associated with cancer screening postponement.

result: Background literature establishes that COVID-19 caused substantial global mortality (6.9M deaths among 677M cases by March 2023), disproportionately affected elderly and those with comorbidities, disrupted cancer care (10% treatment delays), showed racial disparities (2-fold higher hospitalization/death for African Americans), and led to dramatic drops in cancer screening (84.5% for colorectal, 89.2% for breast). Educational attainment is positively associated with cancer screening adherence.
evaluation: Claims C1-C18 cite appropriate prior literature to establish context for the study. The citations appear accurate based on the sources provided (Dong et al., London et al., Newman et al., etc.), though the specific citation dates and statistics should be verified against the original sources. The background appropriately motivates the research question.

result: The study findings are contextualized by prior research showing that U.S. ambulatory care visits declined 60% in early pandemic (February 2020) with partial rebound by April 2020, mammograms/Pap smears dropped 80% and colonoscopies 90% in April 2020, and German studies found postponement associated with chronic disease presence and COVID-19 concern but inversely associated with older age.
evaluation: Claims C74-C81 appropriately cite prior literature (Mehrotra et al., Martin et al., Hajek et al.) to contextualize the study findings. The comparison with German studies (C80-C81) showing inverse age associations with screening postponement aligns with the current study's findings (C68, C92), strengthening the interpretation.

result: The clinical significance of screening delays is established by 5-year survival rates declining dramatically with cancer stage (breast: 99% localized to 27% distant; colorectal: 90% localized to 14% distant), and Canadian modeling studies projecting that 3-6 month screening interruptions could result in hundreds of additional advanced cancers and deaths over the subsequent decade.
evaluation: Claims C82-C87 appropriately cite survival statistics (Siegel et al., 2020) and modeling studies (Yong et al., 2021) to establish the potential clinical consequences of screening delays observed in the study. These citations provide important context for interpreting the public health significance of the findings.

result: The authors conclude that increased monitoring of high-risk patients is critically important given increased risk of undiagnosed cases or poor prognosis from delayed screening/treatment, that their findings are consistent with other pandemic studies, and that the backlog of postponed screenings will have long-term clinical impact and potentially increase cancer burden.
evaluation: Claims C94-C96 represent interpretive conclusions and inferences rather than direct findings. While C95 is supported by the literature comparisons, C94 and C96 are reasonable inferences but go beyond what the cross-sectional survey data can directly demonstrate. The study cannot directly measure long-term clinical impact or cancer burden increases without follow-up data.

result: The study was conducted before COVID-19 vaccines became available (FDA emergency authorization December 10, 2020 was after final baseline survey in September 2020), and very few survey participants (49 men, 68 women) reported having COVID-19 during the baseline survey period.
evaluation: Claims C88 and C97 provide important temporal context for interpreting the findings. The low COVID-19 infection rates among participants (C97) may reflect the effectiveness of the behavioral changes reported, though this is speculative. The pre-vaccine timing (C88) is clearly documented and appropriately noted as a limitation.
